pedagogy.summary: Children learn to describe 3-D solids by three distinct properties — faces, edges and vertices — and to count each for common solids (canonically: a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices). The two teaching challenges are (1) keeping the three properties distinct (a face is a flat 2-D surface, an edge is the straight line where two faces meet, a vertex is the point where edges meet) rather than blurring them under everyday words like 'side' and 'corner', and (2) counting reliably including the hidden features on the far side. It is best taught by handling real solids and counting each property by touch in a fixed order, marking features as they are counted, and being explicit about how curved solids are described.
bestPractices: Count by touch in a fixed order — colour or number each face, trace each edge, dot each vertex — so the three properties stay distinct and nothing is double-counted or missed.
Hand children the real solid to turn while looking at pictures of it, so hidden faces, edges and vertices are included in the count rather than only the visible ones.
Define each term against the object: a face is a flat surface (itself a 2-D shape), an edge is the straight line where two faces meet, a vertex is the corner where edges meet.

Be explicit about curved solids: a curved surface is described as a 'curved surface', not a face, and the curved boundary is not an edge — and note that schemes differ, so state the convention being used.
Connect faces to 2-D shapes and (later) to nets, where each face appears as a separate flat shape, reinforcing the face count.
keyRepresentations: Handleable solids (cube, cuboid, pyramid, sphere, cylinder, cone) counted by touch
Colour-a-face / trace-an-edge / dot-a-vertex marking system while counting
Nets that fold up into the solid, showing each face as a separate 2-D shape
A cube-vs-cylinder pair to contrast flat faces with a curved surface
commonMisconceptions: Blurs faces, edges and vertices under everyday words, calling edges 'sides' and vertices 'corners' so the three properties run together when counting.
Counts only the faces/edges/vertices that are visible, missing the hidden ones on the far side (gives a cube 3 faces, 9 edges or 4 corners).
Counts a curved surface as a 'face' and the curved boundary line as an 'edge' (e.g. says a cylinder has 3 faces).
Treats the whole solid as if it were the 2-D shape of a face, not distinguishing the flat face from the 3-D object.

learn.summary: Children aged 6-7 learn to describe common 3-D solids by three distinct properties — faces (flat surfaces, each itself a 2-D shape), edges (the straight line where two faces meet) and vertices (the corner where edges meet) — and to count each reliably for solids such as a cube (6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices). The two core challenges are keeping the three properties distinct rather than blurring them under everyday words like 'side' and 'corner', and counting the hidden features on the far side rather than only those visible. A well-supported route for this age is handling real solids (including while looking at a flat picture of the same solid), counting each property by touch in a fixed order with a marking system, and being explicit about how curved solids are described.

activities.title: Count a real cube by touch in a fixed order
feedback: If a child calls an edge a 'side' or a vertex a 'corner' and runs the properties together, pause and name each property against the object as they touch it: 'This flat part is a face; this straight line where two faces meet is an edge; this point where edges meet is a vertex.'
If the recount from a different starting face gives a different total, the marking slipped — re-mark systematically so each feature is counted exactly once.
If a child reaches only 3 faces or 9 edges, prompt: 'Turn the cube over — are there features round the back you haven't marked yet?'
activities.rationale: Faces, edges and vertices are spatial properties; counting by touch in a fixed order with a marking system keeps the three distinct and ensures hidden features are included. Handling the real solid while naming each property is a recommended approach for this age.
sourceClaims: A curved surface is NOT a face and the curved line where a curved surface meets a flat face is NOT an edge; each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling solids while viewing images supports counting faces, edges and vertices. Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
KS1/early-years practice: attend to 3-D properties (edges, faces, vertices), handle real objects, and count by physically tracking features; each face relates to a 2-D shape.
learnerActions: Hold a real cube and turn it in your hands.
Count the faces first: colour or number each flat surface as you touch it, saying 'face' each time, until every face is marked. Record the total.
Then trace each edge with a finger, marking each traced edge (e.g. a gold line or sticker), saying 'edge' each time, until all are traced. Record the total.
Then dot each vertex (corner) with a sticker, saying 'vertex' each time. Record the total.
Recount starting from a different face to check your totals stay the same (6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices).
activities.intendedInsight: A face, an edge and a vertex are three different things; counting each property separately in a fixed order, and marking features as you go, keeps them distinct and makes sure nothing hidden is missed or double-counted.

activities.title: Predict then count the hidden features
feedback: A child who predicts around 9 edges (the most you can see at once, when three faces are showing) is reasoning only about the visible faces — celebrate noticing the gap when the far-side edges bring the total to 12. (The '9' is a rough illustrative expectation, not a measured value; from one view you see at most 3 faces, 9 edges and 7 vertices.)

If a child reads all the information straight from the flat picture, prompt them to turn the real solid to check for features the picture hides; the point is linking the 2-D view to the full 3-D object.
If a friend's claim is used ('a cube has 3 faces because they can only see 3'), ask the child to explain, turning the cube, why that friend missed some.
Reinforce that recounting from a different face should reach the same total once hidden features are included.
activities.rationale: Under-counting arises specifically from representing only the visible side of a 3-D figure and difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure; a predict-then-count routine that pairs a flat picture with the real solid and forces attention to the hidden back is intended to target this error.
sourceClaims: Students represent only the visible side of a 3-D figure and under-count features that are not directly visible, reflecting difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure — grounds the hidden-feature under-count when counting faces/edges/vertices.
learnerActions: Before counting, look at a cube and predict out loud how many edges it has altogether, saying your number first.
Look at a flat picture or drawing of the cube next to the real cube, and point out which edges, faces and corners in the picture are hidden from view.
Now trace and mark every edge on the real cube together, turning it so the far side comes into view and you find the hidden features from the picture.
Compare your prediction with the counted total of 12, and talk about the edges 'round the back' you could not see at first.
Repeat the routine for vertices and faces: each time, predict the visible-only number aloud first, then turn the real solid to reach the full totals (8 vertices, 6 faces).
activities.intendedInsight: A solid has features on its hidden far side that a flat picture does not show directly; a count based only on what you can see is too small, so you must turn the real object to catch every feature.

activities.title: Flat face versus curved surface
feedback: If a child says a cylinder has 3 faces, have them feel the round wall and ask whether it is flat like a face — then introduce 'curved surface' for it.
State explicitly which convention you are using, because schemes differ in how they describe curved solids; tell the child the rule you are following so they are not confused by other wording.
Reinforce by linking each flat face to the 2-D shape it matches (the circular faces of the cylinder, the square faces of the cube).
activities.rationale: The curved-surface distinction is an explicit curriculum convention that must be taught directly and stated, since schemes differ; feeling flat versus curved on real solids makes the distinction concrete.
sourceClaims: A curved surface is NOT a face and the curved line where a curved surface meets a flat face is NOT an edge; each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling solids while viewing images supports counting faces, edges and vertices. Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
learnerActions: Hold a cylinder and run a hand over the round wall and over the flat ends.
Count the flat faces — the two circles on a cylinder — and mark them.
Decide whether the round wall is a face: feel that it is not flat, and name it a 'curved surface' rather than a face.
Check the circle-to-curve boundary: is it a straight line where two flat faces meet? Under the convention we are using, if not, it is not counted as an edge (some schemes call it a curved edge).
Say the full description: a cylinder has two flat (circular) faces and one curved surface.
Then repeat with a cone and note it has one flat circular face, one curved surface, and a single pointed apex; say whether your scheme calls the apex a vertex, since no edges meet there.
Compare the solids directly with the cube to contrast flat faces with a curved surface.
activities.intendedInsight: Under the convention used here, a face is a flat surface and an edge is a straight line where two flat faces meet; the round part of a cylinder or cone is described as a curved surface, not a face, and its curved boundary is not counted as an edge, while a cone has a pointed apex that many schemes call a vertex even though no edges meet there.

activities.title: Faces as 2-D shapes and nets
feedback: For a flat-faced solid, if the number of shapes in the net does not match the touch-count of faces, recount both and find the discrepancy together; for curved solids, expect one extra piece that forms the curved surface.
Emphasise that the whole solid is not the same as one of its flat faces — the solid is a 3-D object, each face is a flat 2-D shape.

Note for the adult: a paper or card net has a slight real thickness and is a physical model of the ideal flat faces, which mathematically have no thickness. Ask the child about the flat 2-D shape the card represents (a square, a circle), not whether the card itself can be held or how thick it is.
activities.rationale: Connecting faces to 2-D shapes and to nets, where each face appears as a separate flat shape, reinforces the face count and addresses treating the whole solid as if it were a 2-D shape; the card is an approximation of the ideal flat face and this is made explicit in the activity.
sourceClaims: A curved surface is NOT a face and the curved line where a curved surface meets a flat face is NOT an edge; each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling solids while viewing images supports counting faces, edges and vertices. Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
learnerActions: For a solid you have counted (e.g. a cube), name the 2-D shape of each face (a square).
Unfold a net that folds up into the solid, laying out each face as a separate flat shape.

For a solid with only flat faces (e.g. a cube), count the flat shapes in the net and check the number matches the face count you found by touch; for a cylinder or cone, notice that one piece of the net becomes the curved surface, not a face.
Fold the net back into the solid to see each flat shape become a face.
Talk about the shape each face represents — a square, a circle — rather than about the card itself.
activities.intendedInsight: Each face of a 3-D solid is a 2-D shape; seeing the faces laid out flat in a net, each as its own shape, reinforces the face count and links 3-D solids to 2-D shapes.

activities.title: Check and explain the counts
feedback: Recall questions check the totals but do not by themselves build the counting strategy — if a count is wrong, return to handling and marking the real solid rather than just stating the right number.
A child who can give numbers but cannot say how a face differs from an edge may be reciting; probe the distinction and reteach by touch if needed.
activities.rationale: Direct questions and matching can check recall of counts but do not by themselves build the counting strategy or the face/edge/vertex distinction; they are best used as an end-check alongside asking the child to articulate the difference. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested design.
learnerActions: Answer direct questions such as 'How many edges does a cube have?' and match a solid to its face count.
Explain in your own words what makes a face different from an edge, and an edge different from a vertex.
Respond to a friend's wrong claim (e.g. 'a cube has 3 faces because I can only see 3') by explaining and demonstrating the correct count.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state the counts and articulate the difference between the three properties shows the properties are genuinely held apart, not just recited.

constraints: Tap-to-reveal or labelled-model activities that show a feature's name and definition on tap can teach vocabulary, but they display the answer rather than requiring the child to build the count or feel the flat-versus-curved distinction; use them to introduce terms, not to replace counting.

A flat-screen tally that colours each tapped face/edge/vertex can build the keep-them-distinct skill, but a flat screen makes it harder to reveal hidden features on the far side — a main source of miscounting; pair it with a solid the child can turn.

A rotatable on-screen 3-D model lets a child turn the solid to catch hidden features and can toggle to a cylinder for the curved-surface convention; it is one good way to surface the hidden-feature error, but real solids in the hand should confirm what the screen shows, and the on-screen model should be understood as a model of the solid, not the solid itself.
Scored recall questions check whether a child remembers counts; they do not on their own build the counting strategy or the property distinction, so use them as an end-check.
Always state explicitly which convention you are using for describing curved solids, because schemes differ.

Paper nets and card cutouts have a slight real thickness and are approximations of the ideal flat faces, which have no thickness; use them to represent faces but keep attention on the flat 2-D shape represented rather than on picking up or handling the card as a definition of the shape.
Recognising or recalling counts is not the same as producing a reliable count by handling and tracking features; expect production, not only recognition.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The cited study on under-counting hidden features (Sudirman et al., 2023) used a junior-high sample and documents the general obstacle, not the 6-7 age group specifically; treat its applicability to this age as indicative, not established.

The legacy source material asserted in places that no flat medium can target these challenges and that a 3-D interactive is uniquely necessary; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been softened to scoped affordances and limits.
The 'typically predicts around 9' figure for visible cube edges, and the 'stall at 3 or 4', are illustrative expectations, not measured results; use them as rough guides only.
The hypothetical friend's claim of '4 faces' is a child-level undercount used only as a wrong claim to refute; the correct cube total is 6 faces.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a cube. 'Predict how many edges this cube has altogether. Say your number before we trace them.' A child who counts only what they see typically predicts around 9 (the visible edges). Then trace and mark every edge together, turning the cube. The gap between the predicted number and the counted 12 — and their reaction to the edges 'round the back' — is the diagnostic: it exposes whether they reasoned about the whole solid or only its visible face.
probeDeeper: Here is a cylinder. How many flat faces does it have? Is the round curved part a face? How can you tell?
You counted the corners you can see. Turn the cube over — did you miss any? How many are there altogether?
Show me an edge. Now show me a vertex. What is the difference between them?
A friend says a cube has 4 faces because they can only see 4. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. A face is a flat surface (itself a 2-D shape — here a square); an edge is the straight line where two faces meet; a vertex/corner is the point where edges meet. The child counts systematically — turning the cube and tracking the hidden features — rather than counting only what faces them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Blurs the three properties, using 'side' or 'corner' loosely so face, edge and vertex run together when counting.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count by touch in a fixed order — colour each face, trace each edge, dot each vertex — naming the property each time, so the three stay distinct.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot say what makes a face different from an edge, calls edges 'sides', and gives inconsistent counts when asked to recount.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts only the visible faces/edges/vertices and misses the hidden ones — gives a cube 3 faces or 4 corners.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand them the solid to turn, marking each feature as it is counted (sticker on vertices, line on edges) so hidden ones are included; recount from a different face to confirm the total is stable.
errorPatterns.distractor: A cube has 3 faces and 4 corners.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States fewer than 6 faces / 8 vertices / 12 edges; on questioning, admits counting only what faced them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts a curved surface as a 'face' and the curved boundary line as an 'edge' — e.g. says a cylinder has 3 faces.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Feel the solids: a face is FLAT and an edge is a straight line where two flat faces meet; adopt 'curved surface' language for the round part, and state the scheme's convention explicitly since schemes differ.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a cylinder or cone, counts the curved surface as a face or calls the circle-to-curve boundary an edge.

responseLevels.gap: Blurs faces, edges and vertices (calls edges 'sides', cannot distinguish them) or counts only the visible features, giving inconsistent counts.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes face (flat 2-D surface), edge (line where two faces meet) and vertex (corner where edges meet), counts all three correctly including hidden features by tracking systematically, and transfers the distinction to a new solid — e.g. correctly says a cylinder has two flat faces and a curved surface (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Counts the faces, edges and vertices of a cube correctly when handling it and can define each, but lists the three counts without coordinating them, miscounts hidden features on a less familiar solid, or wrongly counts a curved surface as a face (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a real cube. Ask: 'Count the faces, then the edges, then the corners (vertices). Now tell me — what makes a face different from an edge?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three counts together with the face-vs-edge distinction separate a child who genuinely holds the three properties apart from one who blurs them (calling edges 'sides', miscounting because the properties run together) or who counts only the visible half. Reaching 12 edges in particular requires tracking hidden edges, so it is hard to fluke by looking; the second tier exposes whether the child can articulate the difference or is just reciting numbers.

Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
